When a person dies, their body begins to break down and rot almost immediately. This happens because of bacteria and natural chemical processes inside the body. Left alone, a dead body can decompose quite rapidly.

To embalm a body means to treat it with special preserving chemicals so that it does not decay — or at least decays very slowly. Think of it as a way of "pausing" the natural breakdown of the body.
What Actually Happens When Someone Embalms a Body

A trained professional called an embalmer performs this procedure. Here is what the process generally involves:

  • The blood is drained from the body through the veins.
  • In its place, a preserving chemical fluid — most commonly a solution containing formaldehyde — is pumped into the body through the arteries. This fluid kills bacteria and firms up the body's tissues, slowing down decomposition significantly.
  • The body's internal cavities are also treated with preserving chemicals.
  • Finally, the body is cleaned, dressed, and sometimes cosmetics are applied to make the person look peaceful and natural for a funeral viewing.

The result is a body that can remain preserved and presentable for days, weeks, or sometimes much longer than it would have without treatment.

Embalming serves several practical and cultural purposes:

  • Funerals and viewings: Families often want to see the deceased one last time before burial. Embalming gives them a few days to gather, plan the funeral, and say goodbye — without the body deteriorating during that time.
  • Long-distance transportation: If someone dies far from their hometown or in another country, their body may need to be transported. Embalming ensures the body survives the journey intact.
  • Medical and scientific study: Bodies donated to medical schools for students to study anatomy are embalmed to preserve them for extended periods.
  • Historical and cultural reasons: Ancient Egyptians famously embalmed their dead — a process we know today as mummification. This was done for religious reasons, as they believed the body needed to be preserved for the afterlife.

These examples will help you see how the word is used naturally:

  • "The funeral home staff embalmed the body before the viewing."
  • "The body had been embalmed, so it remained preserved for weeks."
  • "Medical students study embalmed cadavers during anatomy classes."

"Embalm" is sometimes used figuratively — meaning it is used beyond its literal sense to describe preserving something in a fixed, frozen, or unchanging state, often something non-physical like a memory, a tradition, or a moment in time. This usage often carries a slightly melancholic or critical tone, as if the thing being "embalmed" has been kept artificially alive rather than being allowed to grow or change naturally.

Examples:

  • "The old town felt embalmed in the past — nothing had changed in fifty years."
  • "Her journals embalmed the memories of a life she had long left behind."
  • "The institution had embalmed its century-old rules, refusing to adapt to modern times."

In each of these cases, nothing is literally being treated with chemicals. Instead, the word paints a picture of something being preserved so rigidly that it feels lifeless or stuck in time — just like an embalmed body.

• Embalmed — past tense ("The body was embalmed yesterday.")
  • Embalming — present/ongoing action ("The embalming process takes a few hours.")
  • Embalmer — the person who performs the procedure ("She trained for two years to become a licensed embalmer.")
  • Embalmment — the noun referring to the act itself ("Embalmment is required by law in certain situations.")
To embalm is to treat a dead body with preserving chemicals to prevent it from decaying, and — by extension — to figuratively preserve anything in a fixed, unchanging state.
